428.title: Peace of mind
428.hook: tranquility comes from letting go of what isn't yours to control
428.howItsDone: Stoics aim for tranquility by distinguishing what is up to them from what isn't, and by practicing calm in ordinary, noisy situations rather than waiting for quiet ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was my post, the soldier's station, kept well. Your line was stay at it well.

You finally get the quiet weekend. Phone off, a stack of books, a cabin with no signal. Then on Saturday morning a neighbor starts a leaf blower, and keeps it going for an hour. By noon the real trouble isn't the noise. It's the ruined plan for peace and quiet. There's something funny in that, and Epictetus noticed it long before leaf blowers. In book four, chapter four, he tells people who want a calm life that they may be chasing it the wrong way.
screen: `THE QUIET WEEKEND.` → `THE LEAF BLOWER.` → `PEACE OF MIND.`

segments.voice: The Greeks had a name for the calm everyone was after: ataraxia. It's built from a verb for stirring up or troubling, the way you'd stir mud in a pond, with a- in front: not. Ataraxia: unstirred. It wasn't only a Stoic word; Epicureans and Skeptics prized it too, each by its own road. Here's the surprise. Epictetus says wanting leisure, or quiet, or time to read, can make you just as anxious as wanting money or power. If your peace depends on no leaf blowers, then a leaf blower owns your peace. Tranquility wanted as an outside condition is one more thing outside your control. He picks on readers in particular. If you can't read and it upsets you, he asks, what was the reading for? Reading is meant to prepare you for life, not replace it. Someone who reads about calm all day and then snaps at whoever interrupts has missed the point of the book. So for Epictetus, peace of mind isn't a place you get to. It's what's left when you stop demanding that things outside you behave. Your judgments, your choices, your effort are yours. The neighbor's yard tools are not. Let go of the second, and the pond settles by itself, even with the noise still going. Peace of mind isn't silence. It's not being stirred.
screen: `ATARAXIA: UNSTIRRED.` · `WANTING QUIET CAN ENSLAVE YOU.` · `READING IS PRACTICE FOR LIFE.` · `LET GO OF WHAT ISN'T YOURS.` · then, large: `PEACE OF MIND.`

segments.voice: Don't try to make anything quiet; let the sounds around you keep going, traffic, a fridge, a voice in the next room. Each time one pulls at you, notice it and let it be a sound, outside you, not yours to fix. The noise is wind across a pond; rest in the still water underneath.
Ataraxia. Greek for being unstirred: the calm that comes from letting go of what isn't yours to control, not from finding a perfectly quiet place. Today's word.
Your line: not being stirred. The noise can keep going while the pond settles. That's day four hundred twenty-eight.

429.title: Attention, always
429.hook: once you relax your attention, don't think you can pick it back up whenever you like
429.howItsDone: Stoic practice includes prosochē, a steady watchfulness over one's own judgments and actions, renewed many times a day whenever attention slips.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ataraxia, the pond unstirred under the noise. Your line was not being stirred.

You pick up your phone to check one thing, the weather. Twenty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusted frying pan, with no memory of deciding to. You never checked the weather. Epictetus knew this slide, without the phone. Near the end of the Discourses, book four, chapter twelve, there's a short, sharp talk about what happens when you let your attention go, and why getting it back is harder than it looks.
screen: `CHECK THE WEATHER.` → `TWENTY MINUTES LATER: A FRYING PAN.` → `ATTENTION, ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Prosochē is Greek for attention, from a verb meaning to hold toward: to hold the mind toward something. For Epictetus it's the watchfulness under every other practice. You can't sort what's yours from what isn't if you aren't paying attention when the moment comes. His warning: when you relax your attention for a while, don't imagine you can pick it back up whenever you like. Today's slip makes tomorrow's easier. A habit of not attending forms quietly, and then you're always putting it off. Tomorrow I'll be careful, people say. Which means, he points out, that today you won't be. Nothing gets done well without attention, he says, not by the carpenter, not by the person steering a ship. Why would living well be the one craft you could do half asleep? Then the honest part. Can anyone be faultless? No, Epictetus says plainly. What is possible is to keep straining toward not making mistakes. If, by never letting attention go completely, we avoid even a few faults, that's worth having. He isn't asking for perfection. He's asking you to keep showing up to your own life. Later, some Christian monastic writers used prosochē as one of their words for watchfulness of the heart: the same small word, down a different road. Attention isn't something you finish. You return to it, and the returning is the practice.
screen: `PROSOCHĒ: HOLDING THE MIND TOWARD.` · `A SLIP TODAY MAKES TOMORROW'S EASIER.` · `NO CRAFT IS DONE HALF ASLEEP.` · `NOT FAULTLESS: ALWAYS RETURNING.` · then, large: `ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Choose one small task you can do right now, folding a shirt, washing a cup, or simply breathing, and give it all of you: the fabric, the water, the air. When your mind wanders, and it will, notice where it went and bring it back gently, without scolding. Each return is a rep.
Prosochē. Greek for attention, holding the mind toward what's in front of you; for Epictetus, the watchfulness every other practice depends on. Today's word.
Your line: attention. Not faultless, just always coming back to what is in front of you. Day four hundred twenty-nine, done.

430.title: Discourses close
430.hook: forty lessons from a blunt, kind teacher who was once a slave
430.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus reread the Discourses over many years, keeping a few lines close, and some write back to him in journals as if to a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prosochē, attention, the watchfulness you keep coming back to. Your line was attention.

There's a kind of teacher who is hard on a student and obviously on their side. The one who hands back the paper covered in red ink, then stays after class to go through it line by line. The thank-you, if it comes, sometimes comes years later. For more than forty days we've sat in a classroom in Nicopolis with a teacher like that. Today we stand up from the bench, look back at the room, and say goodbye.
screen: `THE RED-INK TEACHER.` → `FORTY DAYS IN NICOPOLIS.` → `THE DISCOURSES CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Epictetus had been enslaved, walked with a lame leg, and in his own talks calls himself a lame old man. He taught at Nicopolis, on the Greek coast. He wrote nothing. What we have, his student Arrian took down: four books of talks, the Discourses. Arrian says in his preface that he tried to keep the teacher's own words, as notes for himself. The voice is blunt. He mocks, teases, calls his students lazy and their excuses silly. He'll press a father who ran from his sick daughter's bedside on whether that was really love. And he's kind the way a good coach is kind: he won't let you be less than you could be. Look at what we carried out of the room: the gift of use, and not even Zeus can take your choice. Money-changer. Sphaira. Onoma. Hexis. Unhindered. Alone, not lonely, a scout, in its season, kosmopolitēs, free is wanting rightly, nothing to take, my post, peace of mind, and yesterday, attention. One idea turned forty ways: some things are ours and some aren't, and freedom lives on the side that's ours. Tomorrow a very different Stoic picks up the thread. Seneca was rich, powerful and close to an emperor, the opposite of a freed slave teaching on the coast, and late in life he wrote letters to a friend. Same porch, new voice. But first, the thank you.

431.title: Letters to a friend
431.hook: late in life, Seneca writes 124 letters to Lucilius, a friend in Sicily, about living well
431.howItsDone: Some readers work through Seneca's letters one at a time, a letter a day, and some keep up the habit of writing reflective letters to a friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epictetus, the blunt, kind teacher whose talks Arrian kept. Your line was thank you, teacher.

Somewhere in a drawer, a shoebox or an old email account, you may have a letter someone wrote only to you. Not a group message. Not a post. A letter with your name at the top, written by someone thinking about you as they wrote. Those are the kind people keep. Long ago, an old and powerful Roman stepped back from public life and started writing letters like that to one friend. People are still reading them.
screen: `A LETTER WITH YOUR NAME ON IT.` → `THE ONES PEOPLE KEEP.` → `LETTERS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a famous writer in Rome. He was exiled, called back, and became tutor and then advisor to the young emperor Nero. He grew very rich. He lived right in the middle of everything the Stoics warned about, and he knew it. The historian Tacitus tells how he finally asked Nero's leave to withdraw from court, and offered to hand back his wealth. Lucilius, the letters tell us, was serving as a Roman official in Sicily, a writer himself, interested in philosophy. Seneca writes to him as an equal a few steps behind on the same path. Every letter opens the same way, in Latin: Seneca to his Lucilius, greetings. A hundred twenty-four survive, written in Seneca's last years. They're short. Each usually takes something ordinary, a trip, a cold bath, a noisy apartment, a visit to an old house, and turns it into a lesson about how to live. Readers still argue whether Lucilius really received them all or Seneca wrote them to be published. Either way, they're written to one person. Later, Tacitus tells us, Nero accused Seneca of a part in a plot against him and ordered him to die. The letters were written with that shadow already falling, which is why they're urgent and tender at once. For the next stretch of the path, we'll read them in order, a letter at a time, as if they were addressed to us.
screen: `SENECA: RICH, POWERFUL, UNEASY.` · `LUCILIUS, A FRIEND IN SICILY.` · `124 SHORT LETTERS ABOUT LIVING.` · `WRITTEN IN THE LAST YEARS.` · then, large: `DEAR FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Think of one friend you haven't really written to in a while, and picture them at their kitchen table, opening something from you. In your head or on paper, begin: dear, and their name, then add two or three sentences: something you noticed, something you've been thinking about, something you hope for them. You don't have to send it; just write to one person, the way Seneca did.

Your line: dear friend. A letter to one person can still be read two thousand years on. Until the next letter.

432.title: Hold every hour
432.hook: take hold of each hour, Seneca begins, and you'll depend less on tomorrow
432.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often keep a simple account of their time, noticing where the day went in the evening, and try to give each hour a purpose before it begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Lucilius, the friend in Sicily Seneca wrote to. Your line was dear friend.

Open the screen-time report on your phone and it will tell you, to the minute, where your week went. Plenty of people look once, wince, and never open it again. Seneca didn't have the report. He had something like it in his own head, and in the very first letter to Lucilius he opens it and makes himself look. The first lesson of a hundred twenty-four isn't about God or virtue. It's about time, and where ours keeps going.

Letter one begins, in Latin, vindica te tibi: claim yourself for yourself. Vindica is a legal word, used for claiming property, or claiming a person's freedom in court. Seneca is telling Lucilius to take himself back, the way you'd take back something taken from you. Then the three thieves. Some of our time, he says, is torn away from us, some is quietly stolen, and some just slips through our fingers. The most shameful loss comes from carelessness. Most of life passes doing the wrong thing, much of it doing nothing, and all of it doing something other than what we meant to. Then the line that names this day. In Gummere's translation: hold every hour in your grasp. Take hold of today's work, Seneca says, and you'll depend less on tomorrow's. Year one gave us the sentence that follows soon after: nothing is ours except time. And Seneca doesn't pretend he's mastered it. He keeps accounts of his own time, he tells Lucilius, the way someone free-handed but careful keeps a household budget. He can't boast that he wastes nothing, but he can say what he's wasting, and why. He's not preaching from a mountaintop. He's a man in his sixties, honest about his losses, and starting today. That's what holding an hour looks like: not a perfect schedule, just taking the next one in your hand.
screen: `VINDICA TE TIBI: CLAIM YOURSELF.` · `TORN AWAY, STOLEN, SLIPPED AWAY.` · `HOLD EVERY HOUR IN YOUR GRASP.` · `SENECA KEEPS HIS OWN ACCOUNTS.` · then, large: `HOLD THIS HOUR.`

segments.voice: Look at the clock and think about the next hour, the real one, not the ideal one, and pick one thing it's for: the report, the walk, the meal with your family, sleep. 433.title: Nowhere and everywhere
433.hook: reading too many authors scatters you: the one who is everywhere is nowhere
433.howItsDone: Readers following Seneca's advice sometimes stay with a few trusted authors, reread rather than skim, and take away one thought each day to carry.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was three thieves: time torn away, stolen, or let slip. Your line was hold this hour.

Fourteen browser tabs. Three half-read books by the bed. Two podcasts paused in the middle. A language app, a cooking channel, a course you paid for in January. None of it bad. All of it started. Very little finished. Seneca's second letter praises Lucilius for not living like that, then warns how easily he could start. We met one line of this letter in year one, about reading slowly. Today we go underneath it, to the restlessness itself.
screen: `FOURTEEN TABS OPEN.` → `ALL STARTED, LITTLE FINISHED.` → `NOWHERE AND EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Seneca opens kindly. He's heard that Lucilius isn't rushing from place to place, and takes it as a sign of a settled mind. A mind in order, he says, can stop and spend time with itself. Then the warning. Be careful that reading many authors and every kind of book doesn't make you as restless as constant travel. In Gummere's translation, three words: Everywhere means nowhere. Seneca piles up pictures. A person who spends life traveling ends up with many acquaintances and no friends. Food that comes straight back up doesn't nourish the body. A wound doesn't heal if you keep changing the medicine. A plant moved again and again can't grow strong roots. Every picture says the same thing: depth needs staying. So stay with a few, Seneca says, and let them sink in. When you feel like a change, go back to someone you've already read. And each day take away one thought to digest. Not because new things are bad. But you can't take root in fourteen places at once. The restless person isn't everywhere. They're nowhere for very long. The one who stays can finally arrive.
screen: `A SETTLED MIND CAN STAY.` · `EVERYWHERE MEANS NOWHERE.` · `THE PLANT MOVED TOO OFTEN.` · `STAY WITH A FEW; DIGEST ONE.` · then, large: `GO DEEP.`

segments.voice: Take one short thing to read, a line you love, a verse, today's line, and read it once at normal speed. Then read it again, slower, as if you'd never seen it, and notice one word you missed the first time. Stay with that word, and let it put down one small root.
Strong roots, what a plant can't grow if it's moved again and again: Seneca's picture for a mind that stays with a few books instead of scattering. Today's word.
Your line: go deep. One thought a day, digested, is plenty. That's day four hundred thirty-three.

434.title: Who is poor
434.hook: the poor person isn't the one with too little but the one who craves more
434.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism ask whether a desire is necessary or merely more, and set their own limit of enough instead of chasing a moving target.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was strong roots, what the plant moved too often can't grow. Your line was go deep.

Ask a friend how much money would make them feel secure, and remember the number. Ask again five years and two raises later. Quite often the number has moved, and it's still a little more than they have. The target walks away as they walk toward it. Seneca wouldn't have been surprised. At the end of his second letter, after telling Lucilius to stay with a few good authors, he hands him a thought he picked up that day, then gives it a twist that sticks.
screen: `HOW MUCH WOULD BE ENOUGH?` → `ALWAYS A LITTLE MORE.` → `WHO IS POOR.`

segments.voice: Seneca says he's been reading Epicurus, founder of a rival school, and found this: contented poverty is an honorable thing. Seneca likes it, then pushes it a step further. If it's contented, it isn't really poverty at all. Then his own line. The poor person isn't the one who has too little. It's the one who craves more. What does it matter, he asks, how much someone has locked in the safe or stored in the barn, how many flocks or how much interest, if they're always eyeing what belongs to someone else and counting what they don't have yet? So what's the right measure of wealth? First, Seneca says, to have what is necessary. Then, to have what is enough. Not a fixed number. A line you draw yourself. One honest note: Seneca wrote this as a very rich man, and Tacitus records a critic in Seneca's own lifetime attacking him for that wealth. We'll come back to that gap. But the idea doesn't depend on the man. Look at the week we've walked: peace of mind, the pond unstirred; attention; thank you, teacher, at the Discourses' close; then Seneca's letters: dear friend, hold this hour, go deep, and now crave less. Different days, one thread. Whoever keeps counting what they don't have yet is poor, whatever is in the safe.
screen: `EPICURUS: CONTENTED POVERTY.` · `POOR IS THE ONE WHO CRAVES MORE.` · `FIRST NECESSARY, THEN ENOUGH.` · `THE WEEK: ONE THREAD.` · then, large: `CRAVE LESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting, new shoes, a bigger place, a little more in the account, and ask Seneca's two questions: is it necessary, and if not, do I already have enough without it? Don't force an answer; let the want soften a little, like a balloon letting out some air, and notice what's already here that's enough for this minute.
Epicurus. The rival philosopher Seneca was reading: his line that contented poverty is honorable, which Seneca pushes further, since the poor person is the one who craves more.
Your line: crave less. First what's necessary, then what's enough. A week walked; see you tomorrow.

original.say: non kwee PA-rum HA-bet, sed kwee ploos KOO-pit, POW-per est
original.note: Latin: not the one who has too little, but the one who craves more, is poor.
